records.quote: Corollary 5.1. Let Y1, Y2 follow (18). If µ1 ≤ µ2, δ1 ≤ δ2, σ1,ii = σ2,ii for all 1 ≤ i ≤ n and σ1,ij ≤ σ2,ij for all 1 ≤ i ≠ j ≤ n, then P(Y1 > a) ≤ P(Y2 > a) holds for all a ∈ R^n. Furthermore, the foregoing inequality is strict if µ1 < µ2, δ1 < δ2, and σ1,ij < σ2,ij for all 1 ≤ i ≠ j ≤ n.
records.family: GLSEn(µ, Σ, δ, ψ, α, β, H), common ψ, α, β, H
records.compared: upper orthant probabilities P(Y > a) of the two vectors

hypotheses.text: µ1 ≤ µ2, δ1 ≤ δ2, σ1,ii = σ2,ii for all 1 ≤ i ≤ n and σ1,ij ≤ σ2,ij for all 1 ≤ i ≠ j ≤ n
hypotheses.formal: componentwise ordering of location, skewness and off-diagonal scale; equal diagonal scale

conclusion.direction: Y1 ≤uo Y2, i.e., P(Y1 > a) ≤ P(Y2 > a) for all a (strict under strict parameter inequalities)

records.quantifiers: all a ∈ R^n; 1 ≤ i ≠ j ≤ n
records.ambiguity: Upper orthant order (extended Slepian theorem); not in the spec's named list, recorded as 'other: uo'. The a_dirs/b_dirs disagreement is an artifact: both passes' records state P(Y1 > a) ≤ P(Y2 > a), i.e., Y1 smaller.

note: Both passes agree on the printed inequality P(Y1 > a) ≤ P(Y2 > a) ∀a; direction code diff is an artifact. Order labeled 'other: uo' (upper orthant).

records.quote: Corollary 5.5. Let Y1, Y2 follow (18), where Σ1 and Σ2 are correlation matrices and n ∈ {2, 3}. Assume µ1 = µ2, δ1 = δ2 and σ1,ij ≤ σ2,ij for all 1 ≤ i < j ≤ n, then Gn(Y2) ≤icx Gn(Y1). [Gn(X) = (1/n²)Σ_{i,j}|Xi − Xj|.]
records.model: other: Gini index of a random vector
records.family: GLSEn with Σ correlation matrices, n ∈ {2,3}
records.compared: Gini indices Gn(Y2) vs Gn(Y1) — reversed icx direction

hypotheses.text: µ1 = µ2, δ1 = δ2 and σ1,ij ≤ σ2,ij for all 1 ≤ i < j ≤ n; Σ1, Σ2 correlation matrices; n ∈ {2,3}
hypotheses.formal: equal marginals + correlation ordering giving Y1 ≤sm Y2 via Corollary 4.13

conclusion.direction: Gn(Y2) ≤icx Gn(Y1) — higher correlation lowers the Gini index in icx

note: Both passes agree: reversed direction Gn(Y2) ≤icx Gn(Y1) is what the paper prints; higher correlation ⇒ smaller Gini index.

records.quote: Example 4.4. We consider the special case of univariate GLSE distribution to illustrate the results in Lemma 4.3. The survival functions of the GHSS distributions under three parameter setting are plotted in Figure 1(a). It is easy to check that the conditions in Lemma 4.3(1) are satisfied, and thus agrees with the usual stochastic ordering among these three distributions displayed in the plot.
records.family: univariate GHSS(µ, σ, δ, λ) distributions

hypotheses.text: conditions in Lemma 4.3(1) are satisfied
hypotheses.formal: µ2 − µ1 + β(z)(δ2 − δ1) ≥ 0 ∀z and σ1 = σ2 for each pair

conclusion.direction: the three GHSS distributions are st-ordered (survival functions nested in Figure 1(a)) — supports Lemma 4.3(1)

records.quote: Moreover, Figure 1(b) provides a counterexample showing that the survival functions of these distributions cross with each other if the scale parameters of the three distributions are not identical.
records.family: univariate GHSS(µ, σ, δ, λ) distributions

hypotheses.text: scale parameters of the three distributions are not identical
hypotheses.formal: violates the σ1 = σ2 requirement of Lemma 4.3(1)

conclusion.direction: no st order: survival functions cross when σ's differ — the σ1 = σ2 hypothesis of Lemma 4.3(1) is essential

records.ambiguity: Parameter triples for panel (b) read from the figure legend.

note: Example 4.4 prints both a supporting example (a, st-ordered) and a counterexample (b, crossing when σ differ); emitted as two records.

records.quote: Example 4.8. As an illustration for Lemma 4.7, the stop-loss transformations for the univariate GHSS distributions are plotted in Figure 2. It is easy to check that the conditions in Lemma 4.7(1) are satisfied, and consistent with the increasing convex ordering among these three distributions displayed by the stop-loss transformations in Figure 2(a).
records.family: univariate GHSS(µ, σ, δ, λ) distributions

hypotheses.text: conditions in Lemma 4.7(1) are satisfied
hypotheses.formal: µ2 − µ1 + β(z)(δ2 − δ1) ≥ 0 ∀z and σ1 ≤ σ2 for each pair

conclusion.direction: the three GHSS distributions are icx-ordered (stop-loss transforms nested in Figure 2(a)) — supports Lemma 4.7(1)

records.quote: Figure 2(b) provides a counterexample under the setting (µ1, σ1, δ1) = (0, 1, 0.5) and (µ2, σ2, δ2) = (1, 2, −0.5). It is clear that size relation between µ2 + β(z)δ2 and µ1 + β(z)δ1 varies with respect to z, meaning that the conditions in Lemma 4.7(1) are not fully satisfied. This agrees with the plots in Figure 2(b) that the stop-loss transformations of these distributions cross with each other.
records.family: univariate GHSS(µ, σ, δ, λ) distributions

hypotheses.text: size relation between µ2 + β(z)δ2 and µ1 + β(z)δ1 varies with respect to z
hypotheses.formal: violates the uniform-in-z location-mixture inequality of Lemma 4.7(1)

conclusion.direction: no icx order: stop-loss transforms cross — the uniform µ + β(z)δ ordering of Lemma 4.7(1) is essential

note: Example 4.8 prints a supporting icx example (a) and a crossing counterexample (b); emitted as two records.

records.quote: Theorem 4.10. Let Y1, Y2 follow (18). The following statements are true: (1) If µ1 = µ2, δ1 = δ2 and Σ2 ≥ Σ1, then Y1 ≤dcx Y2. (2) If µ1 = µ2, then Y1 ≤dcx Y2 if and only if δ1 = δ2 and Σ2 ≥ Σ1. (3) If δ1 = δ2, then Y1 ≤dcx Y2 if and only if µ1 = µ2 and Σ2 ≥ Σ1.

records.quote: Theorem 4.11. Let Y1, Y2 follow (18). The following statements hold: (1) If µ1 = µ2, δ1 = δ2, σ1,ii ≤ σ2,ii for 1 ≤ i ≤ n and σ1,ij = σ2,ij for 1 ≤ i < j ≤ n, then Y1 ≤ccx Y2. (2) If µ1 = µ2, then Y1 ≤ccx Y2 if and only if δ1 = δ2, σ1,ii ≤ σ2,ii for 1 ≤ i ≤ n and σ1,ij = σ2,ij for 1 ≤ i < j ≤ n. (3) If δ1 = δ2, then Y1 ≤ccx Y2 if and only if µ1 = µ2, σ1,ii ≤ σ2,ii for 1 ≤ i ≤ n and σ1,ij = σ2,ij for 1 ≤ i < j ≤ n.

hypotheses.text: µ1 = µ2, δ1 = δ2; σ1,ii ≤ σ2,ii diagonal; σ1,ij = σ2,ij off-diagonal
hypotheses.formal: equal locations/skews + diagonal ordering

conclusion.direction: Y1 <=_ccx Y2 (iff under the stated equalities)
